[prose] Within the framework of biodiversity and conservation studies, species richness is usually the simplest and most intuitive measure for diversity (Magurran 2004). Several diversity indices have been developed to incorporate the relative abundance of species (or the evenness): of these the Simpson index D is intuitively meaningful and provides good diversity estimates (Magurran 2004). Both species richness and (Simpson) diversity have often been used in ecological studies to describe assemblage shifts and they have proven useful tools to assess and monitor changes caused by environmental variability (e.g., Blaum, Seymour, Rossmanith, Schwager, & Jeltsch 2009; Negro, Isaia, Palestrini, Schoenhofer, & Rolando 2010; Schirmel, Timler, & Buchholz, 2011). Apart from these ‘traditional’ diversity measures, the concept of ‘functional diversity’, which integrates information on life-history traits has grown rapidly in recent years in ecological research (Petchey & Gaston 2006; Violle et al. 2007; Il Choi et al. 2010), since the realization that life-history traits also have an important role to play in diversity (Ribera, Dolédec, Downie, & Foster 2001; Da Silva, Aguiar, Niemelä, Sousa, & Serrano 2007; Vandewalle et al., 2010). Zoological studies have mainly applied the trait concept to freshwater and marine environments (Bremner, Rogers, & Frid 2006; Diaz, Alonso, & Gutierrez 2008), but also to terrestrial arthropods (Keil, Dziock, & Storch 2008; Lambeets, Vandengehuchte, Maelfait, & Bonte 2008; Lambeets, Vandegehuchte, Maelfait, & Bonte 2009). Functional diversity concepts can provide a useful approach to

[prose] integrate biodiversity research into the broader context of ecosystem processes and functioning (Loreau 2010), e.g., for productivity (Tilman et al. 1997) or resilience (Folke et al. 2004). Several indices were developed analogously to traditional alpha diversity indices to measure functional diversity or to display functional composition (Petchey & Gaston 2006; Villéger, Mason, & Mouillot 2008; Laliberté & Legendre 2010). In the present study, three indices were used to explore the different facets of functional diversity: functional evenness (FEve) and functional divergence (FDiv) (Villéger et al. 2008) as well as functional dispersion (FDis) (Laliberté & Legendre 2010). Although it has an extensive theoretical and mathematical background (Schleuter, Daufresne, Massol, & Argillier 2010), functional diversity, especially from multiple traits, has rarely been incorporated into ecological studies to date, and little is known in particular about shifts of functional diversity along environmental gradients (Gerisch et al. 2011). However, life-history traits of carabids and spiders have already been successfully integrated into investigations of assemblage shifts (e.g., Lambeets et al. 2008; Lambeets et al. 2009; Il Choi et al. 2010; Vandewalle et al. 2010).

[prose] To detect possible differences in life-history trait composition among successional stages, we applied GLMs with the number of species of a trait category per plot as the dependent variable (e.g., number of very small spider species per plot). To compensate for overdispersion, the standard errors were corrected using a quasi-Poisson model (Zuur, Ieno, Walker, Saveliev, & Smith 2009). In addition, mean body size of carabid beetles and spiders were compared among the five successional stages using one-way ANOVA.

[prose] Most obviously, habitat heterogeneity facilitates niche differentiation in coastal heathlands (Schultz & Finch 1996); this is reflected by a higher functional diversity (FDis) of carabid beetles and spiders in later and structurally more complex successional stages. Our findings therefore emphasize that species richness (and to some extent Simpson diversity) have limited explanatory power for analyzing shifts along environmental gradients, as also found e.g., by Brose (2003), Mallis and Hurd (2005) and Buchholz (2010).

[prose] Boddenlandschaft’ (Western Pomeranian lagoon area) in Northeastern Germany, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania (Fig. 1). The climate is characterized by an average annual temperature of $7 . 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ and an average annual precipitation of 547 mm (Reinhard 1962). An anthropo-zoogenic coastal heathland is situated in the centre of the island $(54^{\circ}32'\mathrm{N},$ 13◦5E; 1–5 m a.s.l.; Fig. 1) on acidic, nutrient-poor and sandy soils (Bauer 1972). This area was traditionally used as grazing ground for domestic animals and for fuel and building material. However, traditional land use decreased at the beginning of the 20th century and ceased totally around the Second World War (Umweltministerium Mecklenburg-Vorpommern 2003). Nowadays it is preserved as an open landscape by several management measures such as shrub clearing, mowing, sod cutting and (since 2004) sheep grazing. Five main stages of (coastal) heathland succession can be found (Remke 2003): (i) open acidic (coastal) dunes (grey dunes) dominated by Corynephorus canescens, Carex arenaria and cryptogams representing the youngest successional stage (G); (ii) dwarf-shrub heath dominated by Calluna vulgaris and Empetrum nigrum, the main vegetation type within the study area (H); (iii) grassy heath, where the majority of the dwarf-shrubs are displaced by tall graminoids, especially by C. arenaria (C); (iv) shrubheathland dominated by Betula pendula, Betula pubescens or Prunus serotina (S); (v) young birch forest, which has developed due to the lack of management during the last 30–40 years, thus representing the oldest successional stage (B). [prose] We used three functional diversity measurements. FDis expresses changes in functional dispersion, FEve for functional evenness and FDiv for functional divergence. FDis is a measure of functional richness, which considers species relative abundances by estimating their dispersion in a multidimensional trait space (Laliberté & Legendre 2010). In the following, we interpret functional dispersion as a measure for functional diversity per se. Life-history trait data (for dispersal, feeding preference/hunting mode) were coded categorically for calculating functional diversity indices except body size. All used indices are distance-based and can be computed for categorical variables (Laliberté & Legendre 2010; Laliberté & Shipley 2010; Schleuter et al. 2010). We computed FDis (Laliberté & Legendre 2010) and FEve and FDiv (Villéger et al. 2008) using the R language package FD (Laliberté & Shipley 2010). Differences in species richness, Simpson diversity and functional diversity indices among the successional stages were tested with generalised linear models (GLMs) using Poisson models for count data and Gaussian error structures and identity link function for indices.

[prose] In total, 3.646 carabid and 9.934 spider individuals were trapped (Appendix A: Table 1). Species richness did not differ among the five successional stages for carabid beetles or spiders (Appendix A: Table 2). In contrast, Simpson diversity differed among the stages for carabids (Fig. 2), while no differences were observed for spiders (Appendix A: Table 2). [prose] Most carabids specialized in feeding on Collembola occurred in older successional stages, these being shady and more humid habitats that presumably favor higher Collembolan abundances. Active hunting spiders were dominant in open grey dunes, as previously shown by Finch (1997). Due to lower spatial resistance active hunting species, such as Lycosidae, are favored, while ambush and web hunters require well-developed habitat architecture, which is usually not given in grey dunes.
